questions.title: Left ventricular receptors as dual-modality sensors
questions.question: Which of the following is both mechano-receptor & chemo-receptor?

explanations.A: Correct. Unlike the arterial baroreceptors, which are pure mechanoreceptors, and the peripheral chemoreceptors, which are pure chemoreceptors, sensory receptors in the wall of the left ventricle are unusual in responding to both mechanical stimuli, such as distension or stretch of the ventricular wall, and chemical stimuli, such as local accumulation of metabolites or substances reaching the coronary circulation during myocardial ischaemia. Vagal afferent stimulation of these ventricular receptors produces the Bezold-Jarisch reflex, a triad of bradycardia, hypotension and coronary vasodilation. This dual mechanical-and-chemical sensitivity is what distinguishes left ventricular receptors from every other cardiovascular receptor named among the options.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Arterial baroreceptors are stretch receptors only, responding purely to mechanical distension of the vessel wall, with no direct chemical sensitivity.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Atrial receptors (volume receptors) are also mechanoreceptors, responding to stretch from central venous pressure, not to chemical stimuli.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peripheral chemoreceptors are pure chemoreceptors, sensitive to blood gases and pH in the carotid and aortic bodies, with no direct mechanical (stretch) sensitivity of their own.

questions.title: Vasoconstrictor centre location
questions.question: The Vasoconstrictor Center (VCC) is part of which medullary area?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The depressor area inhibits the pressor area's output rather than containing the vasoconstrictor centre itself; it produces vasodilation by inhibition, not by housing the VCC.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The cardiac inhibitory centre is a separate structure that sends vagal efferents to slow heart rate, not the location of the vasoconstrictor centre.
explanations.C: Correct. The medullary vasomotor centre is divided into a pressor area, which contains the vasoconstrictor centre (VCC) and generates the tonic sympathetic discharge that maintains vasomotor tone and raises arterial pressure when activated, and a depressor area, which inhibits the pressor area's own output rather than actively vasodilating by its own efferent output. The VCC's placement within the pressor area is why activating the pressor area raises resistance and pressure, while activating the depressor area lowers them by suppressing that same pressor output.
explanations.D: Incorrect. There is no separate "Vasodilator Center" as such; vasodilation is produced by the depressor area inhibiting the pressor area, not by a distinct vasodilator centre of its own.

questions.title: Cardiac inhibitory centre and vagal outflow
questions.question: Which center sends impulses via the vagus nerve to decrease heart rate?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cardiac stimulatory (accelerator) centre raises, rather than lowers, heart rate and contractility, acting via sympathetic outflow, not the vagus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The vasoconstrictor centre acts on peripheral vascular resistance via sympathetic outflow to blood vessels, not on heart rate via the vagus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. There is no separate vasodilator centre with its own efferent output; vasodilation arises from the depressor area inhibiting the pressor area, not from vagal cardiac outflow.
explanations.D: Correct. A separate cardiac inhibitory centre (CIC), closely linked to the vasomotor centre and to the nucleus of the tractus solitarius which relays baroreceptor and chemoreceptor afferents, sends parasympathetic (vagal) efferent impulses to the heart's sinoatrial node, slowing heart rate when activated. This is distinct from the pressor area's vasoconstrictor centre, which controls vascular resistance via sympathetic outflow rather than heart rate via the vagus, so the two centres divide cardiovascular control between vessel tone and heart rate respectively.

questions.title: Bezold-Jarisch (coronary chemoreflex) effects
questions.question: The Bazold-Jarish reflex (coronary chemoreflex) results in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Tachycardia and hypertension describe a typical sympathetic pressor response, the opposite of the paradoxical reflex tested here.
explanations.B: Correct. Vagal afferent stimulation of the left ventricle's mechano- and chemoreceptors produces the Bezold-Jarisch reflex, also called the coronary chemoreflex: a triad of bradycardia, hypotension and coronary vasodilation, the opposite of the usual sympathetic response to a fall in pressure. It is mediated by a sudden surge of parasympathetic (vagal) outflow to the heart and withdrawal of sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone. Clinically this reflex is invoked to explain the bradycardia and hypotension that can accompany inferior myocardial infarction or reperfusion of an ischaemic coronary territory.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The reflex is characterised by coronary vasodilation, not isolated vasoconstriction, alongside its bradycardic and hypotensive effects.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bradycardia and hypotension together tend to reduce, not increase, cardiac output during this reflex.

questions.title: Most important long-term ABP mechanism
questions.question: The most important mechanism for the long-term regulation of arterial blood pressure is the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The nervous mechanism (baroreceptor and chemoreceptor reflexes) acts within seconds and is the rapid, short-term regulator of arterial pressure, not the most important long-term one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The capillary fluid shift mechanism buffers pressure changes over minutes by shifting fluid between plasma and interstitium; it is not the dominant long-term regulator.
explanations.C: Correct. Long-term arterial blood pressure is regulated mainly by renal and endocrine mechanisms that control extracellular fluid volume: a fall in pressure triggers renin secretion and angiotensin II formation, which raises pressure by vasoconstriction and by promoting renal sodium and water retention, while a rise in pressure and volume triggers ANP secretion, which increases renal sodium excretion, and the kidney's own pressure-natriuresis mechanism directly links arterial pressure to sodium and water excretion. Because these renal mechanisms act over hours to days and can fully correct a sustained pressure disturbance, whereas the nervous mechanism adapts (resets) within days, the renal mechanism is taught as the single most important long-term regulator.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The chemoreceptor mechanism is part of the rapid nervous reflex system, driven by blood gas and pH changes, not the dominant long-term regulator of arterial pressure.

questions.title: Pressure natriuresis definition
questions.question: "Pressure natriuresis" refers to:

options.A: Decreased sodium excretion when pressure is high
options.B: Increased sodium excretion when pressure is high
options.C: Renin secretion when pressure is low

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pressure natriuresis describes increased, not decreased, sodium excretion when arterial pressure rises; a decrease would work against, rather than correct, a high pressure.
explanations.B: Correct. Pressure natriuresis is the kidney's direct link between arterial pressure and sodium excretion: when arterial pressure rises, the kidney excretes more sodium (and water with it), reducing extracellular fluid volume and returning blood pressure toward normal. Atrial natriuretic peptide, secreted in response to atrial stretch from a rising central blood volume, enhances the activity of this pressure-natriuresis mechanism, reinforcing the same corrective direction. This mechanism is a core part of the kidney's role as the body's long-term arterial-pressure regulator.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Renin secretion in response to low pressure is a separate part of the renin-angiotensin system, not what the term pressure natriuresis itself describes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vasoconstriction when pressure is low is a nervous and hormonal (angiotensin II) response, not the renal sodium-excretion mechanism pressure natriuresis names.

questions.learning_objective: Define pressure natriuresis as increased renal sodium excretion when arterial pressure rises.

questions.title: Angiotensin II actions - the exception
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a primary action of Angiotensin II?

options.D: Promotion of sodium and water excretion

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is a genuine action). Angiotensin II raises arterial pressure acutely by direct systemic vasoconstriction, one of its principal, well-established effects.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is a genuine action). Angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex, which then promotes renal sodium retention.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this is a genuine action). Rising angiotensin II, via the pressure rise it produces and direct feedback, suppresses further renin secretion, the normal negative-feedback closure of the renin-angiotensin loop.
explanations.D: Correct. Angiotensin II raises arterial pressure by systemic vasoconstriction and by stimulating aldosterone and ADH secretion, both of which reduce, not promote, renal sodium and water excretion, favouring retention instead. Promotion of sodium and water excretion is precisely the opposing action of atrial natriuretic peptide, not of angiotensin II, which is why this option is the one NOT among angiotensin II's own primary actions.

questions.title: ANP trigger revisited
questions.question: Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP) is secreted in response to:

options.B: Stretching of the atrial muscle fibers

explanations.A: Incorrect. Low blood volume tends to reduce atrial stretch and would suppress, rather than trigger, ANP secretion.
explanations.B: Correct. An increased extracellular fluid volume stretches the atrial muscle fibres, and this stretch of the atrial muscle fibres is the direct trigger that leads to ANP secretion. ANP then increases renal sodium excretion and enhances the pressure-natriuresis mechanism, working to return extracellular fluid volume and blood pressure toward normal. This atrial-stretch trigger is the same fact tested from the Blood Flow section of this paper, confirming atrial stretch, not blood volume or sodium concentration directly, as ANP's proximate stimulus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. ANP's trigger is mechanical atrial stretch, not a chemical sodium-concentration sensor; low sodium concentration is not the described stimulus for its release.
explanations.D: Incorrect. High angiotensin II levels are not the trigger for ANP secretion; if anything, ANP and angiotensin II act as physiological opposites rather than one triggering the other.

questions.learning_objective: State that stretching of the atrial muscle fibres from increased extracellular fluid volume is the trigger for ANP secretion.

questions.title: Vasopressin mechanism of blood pressure regulation
questions.question: Vasopressin (ADH) helps regulate blood pressure by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Vasopressin's vascular action, at higher concentrations, is vasoconstriction, not vasodilation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Vasopressin decreases, rather than increases, renal water excretion, and its principal renal action concerns water rather than sodium handling.
explanations.C: Correct. A decreased extracellular fluid volume reduces the discharge of atrial low-pressure receptors, and this leads to increased secretion of vasopressin, which decreases renal water excretion, that is, promotes water retention, to limit any further fall in extracellular fluid volume and arterial pressure. This water-conserving action is vasopressin's principal contribution to blood-pressure regulation, working alongside the renin-angiotensin system and ANP as one of the three renal/endocrine mechanisms of long-term arterial pressure control.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vasopressin's regulatory action on blood pressure is via water retention and, at higher levels, direct vasoconstriction, not via a direct effect on heart rate.

questions.learning_objective: State that vasopressin regulates blood pressure principally through renal water retention.
